messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mina, a 38-year-old South Eastern Asian stock broker in a long-term relationship, came to treatment describing how a period of stalking had split her life into a before and after. The harassment had begun in a way she initially tried to dismiss: a man she barely knew started appearing near her office building and at the café where she stopped for coffee before the market opened, first with small comments that felt intrusive and then with a steadier pattern of watching, waiting, and leaving messages that made it clear he knew her routines. When the stalking escalated into late-night calls, letters slipped into the lobby of her apartment, and unexplained appearances near the train station, Mina became preoccupied with the feeling that she was being tracked everywhere she went. What stayed with her most was the terror of realizing that ordinary places — the elevator in her building, the sidewalk outside work, the platform during her commute — no longer felt private or safe. Even now, she could describe the original fear with unsettling clarity, yet she also said that the memory felt strangely unreal, “too extreme to be my life,” as though it belonged to someone else. At times, when she tried to remember what happened, the scene did not stay in the past; it came back with such force that she felt as if she were there again, and the same terror rushed through her body with it.

Afterward, Mina found that the memory itself became the gateway to the triggers that now ruled so much of her day. If a sound in the street slammed sharply — a truck door, a dropped pan, a sudden shout from another desk in the trading floor — it could jolt her straight back into the old fear, because the stalking had taught her that an ordinary moment could turn threatening without warning. The smell of alcohol, especially on crowded evenings or in the bar area near her building, carried the same power; it reminded her of the nights when she had been too afraid to be out alone and would scan faces, convinced he might be nearby. Even happy families could unsettle her in a different way. Seeing parents with children, or couples moving easily together through a park, pulled at a painful contrast with the isolation she felt during the stalking, when she had believed that other people moved through a protected world she could not enter. Those scenes were not dangerous in themselves, but because the memory returned to her with such immediacy, they became sharpened by it, and each one could reopen the sense that danger might be closing in again.

Over the following months, Mina became more careful in ways that were easy for others to miss at first. She changed the route she took to work, avoided the café where she had once met colleagues before the opening bell, and started timing her departures so she would not be alone in the lobby at night. At the office she kept her phone face down and her posture rigid, listening for any abrupt noise that might make her heart leap. She noticed that she was no longer enjoying lunches with coworkers when they talked about weekend outings with their children or showed photos of family gatherings; those conversations left her feeling tense and strangely apart, as if she were looking at a life that had been taken from her. Her relationship, too, had become constrained by what she felt she had to monitor and control. She did not want her partner to worry, but she found herself scanning his reactions, checking exits when they went out, and stepping away if someone nearby smelled of alcohol. The more the memory came back in full force, the more closely she watched for anything that might resemble it, and the more her world narrowed around the expectation that another intrusion could happen at any moment.

By the time she sought help, Mina was exhausted by the effort of staying ahead of reminders she could not fully avoid. What finally brought her in was a recent afternoon on the trading floor when a slammed door and a whiff of alcohol from a nearby client’s breath left her shaking, unable to concentrate, and desperate to leave. She said she was tired of feeling as though the stalking were still happening inside her body, tired of the way remembering could make it feel immediate again, and afraid that she was beginning to lose the ordinary ease of her life. What she most hoped for was to be able to pass a loud street, see a happy family, or catch the smell of alcohol without being pulled back into that old terror.
